## Proof

**Claim:** The implication is **false** in general. A prime $P$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ splitting completely in $L=K(\alpha)$ does **not** necessarily force $f(x)\bmod P$ to decompose into $\deg(f)$ distinct linear factors. The obstruction is the index $[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$.

### Background: Dedekind–Kummer

The standard theorem states: if $P\nmid [\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$, then the factorization of $f\bmod P$ into irreducibles $f\equiv\prod \bar g_i^{e_i}$ corresponds bijectively to the factorization $P\mathcal{O}_L=\prod\mathfrak{q_i}^{e_i}$ with $\deg\bar g_i=f(\mathfrak q_i/P)$. In particular, if $P$ splits completely (all $e_i=1$, all residue degrees $1$) **and** $P\nmid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$, then $f\bmod P=\prod$ of $\deg(f)$ distinct linear factors.

When $P\mid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$, this correspondence breaks, and the conclusion can fail. We exhibit an explicit counterexample.

### Counterexample (Dedekind's example)

Let $K=\mathbb{Q}$, $f(x)=x^{3}-x^{2}-2x-8\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and $\alpha$ a root, $L=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$.

**$f$ is irreducible.** Rational root test on $\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8\}$: $f(1)=-10,\ f(-1)=-8,\ f(2)=-8,\ f(-2)=-16,\ f(4)=32,\ f(-4)=-80,\ f(8)=424,\ f(-8)=-568$. No rational root, so the cubic is irreducible. Thus $[L:\mathbb{Q}]=\deg f=3$.

**Discriminant and index.** With $a=-1,b=-2,c=-8$:
$$\operatorname{disc}(f)=a^{2}b^{2}-4b^{3}-4a^{3}c-27c^{2}+18abc=4+32-32-1728-288=-2012=-4\cdot 503.$$
Since $503$ is prime ($\sqrt{503}\approx22.4$, no prime $\le 22$ divides it) and $-503\equiv1\pmod 4$, the field discriminant is $\operatorname{disc}(L)=-503$, giving
$$[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]^{2}=\operatorname{disc}(f)/\operatorname{disc}(L)=4,\qquad [\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]=2.$$
So $2\mid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]$.

**Integral basis.** Set $\beta=(\alpha^{2}+\alpha)/2$. Using $\operatorname{Tr}(1)=3,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)=1,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^{2})=5,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^{3})=31,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^{4})=49$:
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)=3,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha\beta)=18,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\beta^{2})=29,$$
all integers, so $\beta\in\mathcal{O}_L$. The basis $\{1,\alpha,\beta\}$ has discriminant
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}3&1&3\\1&5&18\\3&18&29\end{pmatrix}=3(145-324)-(29-54)+3(18-15)=-537+25+9=-503,$$
confirming $\{1,\alpha,\beta\}$ is an integral basis. The multiplication table is
$$\alpha^{2}=2\beta-\alpha,\qquad \alpha\beta=2\beta+4,\qquad \beta^{2}=2\alpha+3\beta+6.$$

**The prime $2$ splits completely in $L$.** Reduce the multiplication table mod $2$ (writing $\bar\alpha,\bar\beta$):
$$\bar\alpha^{2}=\bar\alpha,\qquad \bar\alpha\bar\beta=0,\qquad \bar\beta^{2}=\bar\beta.$$
So $\mathcal{O}_L/2\mathcal{O}_L\cong\mathbb{F}_2[\bar\alpha,\bar\beta]/(\bar\alpha^{2}-\bar\alpha,\ \bar\beta^{2}-\bar\beta,\ \bar\alpha\bar\beta)$. Define
$$e_1=\bar\alpha,\qquad e_2=\bar\beta,\qquad e_3=1+\bar\alpha+\bar\beta.$$
One checks $e_i^{2}=e_i$, $e_ie_j=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $e_1+e_2+e_3=1$. Hence
$$\mathcal{O}_L/2\mathcal{O}_L\cong\mathbb{F}_2 e_1\oplus\mathbb{F}_2 e_2\oplus\mathbb{F}_2 e_3\cong\mathbb{F}_2\times\mathbb{F}_2\times\mathbb{F}_2.$$
Since $\operatorname{disc}(L)=-503$ is odd, $2$ is unramified. Three copies of $\mathbb{F}_2$ means
$$(2)=\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3,\qquad f(\mathfrak p_i/2)=1\ \forall i,$$
i.e. **$2$ splits completely in $L$**.

**But $f\bmod 2$ is not separable.** 
$$f(x)\bmod 2=x^{3}+x^{2}=x^{2}(x+1),$$
which has a repeated root at $0$ and is **not** separable, and certainly does not decompose into $3$ distinct linear factors (indeed $\mathbb{F}_2$ has only $2$ elements, so three distinct linear factors are *a priori* impossible).

### Conclusion

We have a number field $K=\mathbb{Q}$, an irreducible $f\in\mathcal{O}_K[x]$ of degree $3$, and a prime $P=(2)$ that **splits completely** in $L=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$, yet $f\bmod P=x^{2}(x+1)$ is **not separable** and does **not** decompose into $\deg(f)=3$ distinct linear factors.

The implication fails precisely because $P\mid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$. The correct statement is:

> $f\bmod P$ decomposes into $\deg(f)$ distinct linear factors (and is separable) **if** $P$ splits completely in $L$ **and** $P\nmid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$.

Without the index condition, the answer to the question is **no**.

## Proof

**Claim:** The implication is **false** in general. A prime $P$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ splitting completely in $L=K(\alpha)$ does **not** necessarily force $f(x)\bmod P$ to decompose into $\deg(f)$ distinct linear factors. The obstruction is the index $[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$.

### Background: Dedekind–Kummer

The standard theorem states: if $P\nmid [\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$, then the factorization of $f\bmod P$ into irreducibles $f\equiv\prod \bar g_i^{e_i}$ corresponds bijectively to the factorization $P\mathcal{O}_L=\prod\mathfrak{q_i}^{e_i}$ with $\deg\bar g_i=f(\mathfrak q_i/P)$. In particular, if $P$ splits completely (all $e_i=1$, all residue degrees $1$) **and** $P\nmid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$, then $f\bmod P=\prod$ of $\deg(f)$ distinct linear factors.

When $P\mid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$, this correspondence breaks, and the conclusion can fail. We exhibit an explicit counterexample.

### Counterexample (Dedekind's example)

Let $K=\mathbb{Q}$, $f(x)=x^{3}-x^{2}-2x-8\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and $\alpha$ a root, $L=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$.

**$f$ is irreducible.** Rational root test on $\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8\}$: $f(1)=-10,\ f(-1)=-8,\ f(2)=-8,\ f(-2)=-16,\ f(4)=32,\ f(-4)=-80,\ f(8)=424,\ f(-8)=-568$. No rational root, so the cubic is irreducible. Thus $[L:\mathbb{Q}]=\deg f=3$.

**Discriminant and index.** With $a=-1,b=-2,c=-8$:
$$\operatorname{disc}(f)=a^{2}b^{2}-4b^{3}-4a^{3}c-27c^{2}+18abc=4+32-32-1728-288=-2012=-4\cdot 503.$$
Since $503$ is prime ($\sqrt{503}\approx22.4$, no prime $\le 22$ divides it) and $-503\equiv1\pmod 4$, the field discriminant is $\operatorname{disc}(L)=-503$, giving
$$[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]^{2}=\operatorname{disc}(f)/\operatorname{disc}(L)=4,\qquad [\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]=2.$$
So $2\mid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]$.

**Integral basis.** Set $\beta=(\alpha^{2}+\alpha)/2$. Using $\operatorname{Tr}(1)=3,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)=1,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^{2})=5,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^{3})=31,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^{4})=49$:
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)=3,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha\beta)=18,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\beta^{2})=29,$$
all integers, so $\beta\in\mathcal{O}_L$. The basis $\{1,\alpha,\beta\}$ has discriminant
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}3&1&3\\1&5&18\\3&18&29\end{pmatrix}=3(145-324)-(29-54)+3(18-15)=-537+25+9=-503,$$
confirming $\{1,\alpha,\beta\}$ is an integral basis. The multiplication table is
$$\alpha^{2}=2\beta-\alpha,\qquad \alpha\beta=2\beta+4,\qquad \beta^{2}=2\alpha+3\beta+6.$$

**The prime $2$ splits completely in $L$.** Reduce the multiplication table mod $2$ (writing $\bar\alpha,\bar\beta$):
$$\bar\alpha^{2}=\bar\alpha,\qquad \bar\alpha\bar\beta=0,\qquad \bar\beta^{2}=\bar\beta.$$
So $\mathcal{O}_L/2\mathcal{O}_L\cong\mathbb{F}_2[\bar\alpha,\bar\beta]/(\bar\alpha^{2}-\bar\alpha,\ \bar\beta^{2}-\bar\beta,\ \bar\alpha\bar\beta)$. Define
$$e_1=\bar\alpha,\qquad e_2=\bar\beta,\qquad e_3=1+\bar\alpha+\bar\beta.$$
One checks $e_i^{2}=e_i$, $e_ie_j=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $e_1+e_2+e_3=1$. Hence
$$\mathcal{O}_L/2\mathcal{O}_L\cong\mathbb{F}_2 e_1\oplus\mathbb{F}_2 e_2\oplus\mathbb{F}_2 e_3\cong\mathbb{F}_2\times\mathbb{F}_2\times\mathbb{F}_2.$$
Since $\operatorname{disc}(L)=-503$ is odd, $2$ is unramified. Three copies of $\mathbb{F}_2$ means
$$(2)=\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3,\qquad f(\mathfrak p_i/2)=1\ \forall i,$$
i.e. **$2$ splits completely in $L$**.

**But $f\bmod 2$ is not separable.** 
$$f(x)\bmod 2=x^{3}+x^{2}=x^{2}(x+1),$$
which has a repeated root at $0$ and is **not** separable, and certainly does not decompose into $3$ distinct linear factors (indeed $\mathbb{F}_2$ has only $2$ elements, so three distinct linear factors are *a priori* impossible).

### Conclusion

We have a number field $K=\mathbb{Q}$, an irreducible $f\in\mathcal{O}_K[x]$ of degree $3$, and a prime $P=(2)$ that **splits completely** in $L=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$, yet $f\bmod P=x^{2}(x+1)$ is **not separable** and does **not** decompose into $\deg(f)=3$ distinct linear factors.

The implication fails precisely because $P\mid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$. The correct statement is:

> $f\bmod P$ decomposes into $\deg(f)$ distinct linear factors (and is separable) **if** $P$ splits completely in $L$ **and** $P\nmid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathcal{O}_K[\alpha]]$.

Without the index condition, the answer to the question is **no**.
